images.alt: Original medical illustration of a walking person with visible muscle fibers and colored molecular streams extending toward the brain, heart, liver, gut, and immune cells.
images.caption: Cover illustration. Movement influences multiple body systems. The molecular connections are conceptual and do not depict pathways established by a single experiment.

images.article_section: After Your muscles are more than motors
images.alt: Conceptual diagram showing a contracting muscle, molecules circulating in blood, and possible links with metabolic, immune, and nervous-system tissues.
images.caption: Figure 1. Muscle is part of a whole-body signaling network. This diagram is a conceptual overview of exercise-related communication, not a map of experimentally proven organ-to-organ messages in the 2026 study.

images.article_section: Within What scientists found in 2026, after results
images.alt: Sampling timeline showing 45 minutes of cycling, the plasma and saliva collections before and up to 24 hours after exercise, and the more limited urine collection times.
images.caption: Figure 2. How the 2026 protein atlas was constructed. Time points are shown as equally spaced positions for readability, not as a proportional time axis. The 3,007 count refers to proteins significantly changed immediately after exercise across the tested body fluids.

images.article_section: Within How moving muscles help manage glucose
images.alt: Simplified two-pathway diagram: insulin signaling and muscle contraction both support GLUT4 movement to the muscle-cell membrane, allowing glucose to enter.
images.caption: Figure 3. Two routes to the glucose gateway. Insulin and muscle contraction engage partly distinct signaling pathways that promote GLUT4 movement to the muscle-cell surface. Many intermediate steps are omitted in this educational illustration.
